chapter: Chapter 6: Measurement and Physical Properties of Substances
passage: Apparatus & Materials: A 250 ml glass beaker, a strip of Whatman filter paper (or blotting paper), blue writing ink, a pencil, a ruler, and water. Procedure: 1. Take a rectangular strip of filter paper measuring approximately 15 cm in length and 2 cm in width. 2. Using a pencil, draw a light horizontal line across the strip about 2 cm above the bottom edge. 3. Place a small concentrated drop of blue ink in the center of this line using a fine dropper or nib and let it dry. 4. Pour a small quantity of water into the beaker so that it reaches a depth of about 1 cm. 5. Suspend the paper strip vertically inside the beaker so the bottom edge dips into the water, but the ink spot remains strictly above water. 6. Observe as water climbs up the paper strip through capillary action. 7. The original blue spot separates into distinct colored bands at different heights. Learning Connection: The different dye components of ink have different solubilities in water and different adsorption to paper fibers. The more soluble component ascends faster and reaches a greater height. This proves ink is a mixture of multiple distinct pigments.
evaluation_notes: VALID_METHOD: Full sequential procedure with apparatus, active student observation, and explicit causal link between differential migration and mixture composition.

chapter: Chapter 19: Properties of a Magnetic Field
passage: Materials: A strong bar magnet, a stiff sheet of white cardboard, fine iron filings, a sifter. Instructional Procedure: 1. Place a strong bar magnet horizontally in the center of a wooden table. 2. Place a sheet of smooth white cardboard directly over the bar magnet. 3. Using a fine sifter, sprinkle iron filings evenly and thinly over the entire surface of the cardboard. 4. Instruct students to gently tap the edge of the cardboard with a fingertip 3 to 4 times. 5. Direct student observation: Notice how the scattered iron filings immediately twist and arrange themselves into distinct, continuous curved lines stretching from one pole of the magnet to the other. 6. Guide students to observe the concentration of lines at the North and South poles compared to the center. Learning Connection: Each iron filing becomes an induced magnetic dipole and aligns along the direction of the magnetic field vector. The curved paths visualize lines of magnetic force and demonstrate that magnetic field intensity is strongest near the poles.
evaluation_notes: VALID_METHOD: Concrete instructional procedure with physical apparatus, tactile tapping action, active pattern observation, and explicit mapping to magnetic field vectors.

passage: Materials & Instruments: Compass box containing ruler, pencil, compass with sharp pencil tip, and blank paper. Step-by-step Construction Procedure: 1. Draw any angle ∠ABC of measure 70° on the paper using a protractor and ruler. 2. Place the metallic point of the compass at vertex B. Taking any convenient radius, draw an arc to cut ray BA at point P and ray BC at point Q. 3. Now, place the point of the compass at point P. Taking a radius more than half the distance between P and Q, draw an arc inside the angle. 4. Without changing the radius, place the compass point at point Q and draw another arc intersecting the previous arc. Name the point of intersection as O. 5. Draw a straight ray from vertex B passing through point O using a ruler. Ray BO is the required angle bisector of ∠ABC. 6. Verification: Measure ∠ABO and ∠CBO using a protractor. Both angles measure exactly 35°, demonstrating that ray BO bisects ∠ABC into two congruent angles. Mathematical Principle & Learning Connection: Points on the angle bisector are equidistant from the two arms of the angle. By maintaining equal radii from points P and Q, point O forms two congruent triangles (ΔBPO ≅ ΔBQO by SSS congruence), ensuring ∠PBO = ∠QBO.
evaluation_notes: VALID_METHOD: Full step-by-step geometric construction routine with explicit materials, precise mathematical procedure, student verification step, and underlying geometric rationale.
